title: Mofang
summary: Mofang is a cyber espionage cluster that MITRE ATT&CK describes as likely China based, and it takes its name from a habit that makes it awkward to investigate: it imitates the network infrastructure of the organisations it targets. Public reporting collected there places its activity from at least May 2012, with focused attacks against government and critical infrastructure in Myanmar and against military, automobile and weapons sector organisations in several other countries. The delivery pattern is conventional spear phishing. Reported lures are email attachments in common business formats such as documents, spreadsheets and portable document files, or messages carrying a link to a site the intruders already control, and both routes depend on the recipient opening the file or clicking through. Payloads are compressed inside the attachment and encrypted before download, so static file inspection of the mail attachment alone rarely reveals the final tool. Reporting on the associated remote access family describes behaviour rather than a single fixed signature: user account control bypass, installation as a Windows service, registry run keys for persistence, application shimming as an execution trigger, an external proxy for network traffic, and masqueraded task or service names that imitate legitimate software. Evidence is spread across mail gateway logs, endpoint process ancestry, and service creation records. The important misunderstanding is that infrastructure imitation is not only a branding trick: when an adversary reuses your naming and address conventions, indicators that look like your own network can appear in third party detections, and analysts may wrongly dismiss them as internal noise.

beginner.definition: Mofang is the name for a spying group that public reports link to China. It has been active since about 2012. It is known for copying the network setup of the organisations it attacks. Its targets have included government offices and factories in several countries.
beginner.whyItMatters: The group goes after plans, designs and government information. It usually arrives inside an email attachment that looks like a normal business file. Because it copies the victim's own network details, its activity can look like normal internal traffic. That makes it easy to dismiss as a false alarm. If analysts assume anything familiar is safe, the intrusion can continue for a long time.
howItWorks: The intruders study the target and copy details of its network and naming style.
They send an email with a familiar looking document attached, or a link to a fake page.
The person opens the file or clicks the link, and hidden code starts to run quietly.
The hidden code unpacks and starts a small program that runs in the background.
That program sets itself to start again after a restart and copies files from the computer.
It talks to outside servers, sometimes through another company's computer, so traffic looks normal.
beginner.example: Think of a warehouse where every deliverer wears a numbered vest. A thief makes a vest with the same number as a real driver and walks in with an empty trolley. Staff see the number and assume the delivery is expected. Nothing in the building looks unusual, because the thief copied the one detail people trust. Later, the cameras show a correct looking vest and nobody can name the person wearing it. Network imitation works the same way. The intruder borrows the addresses and names your own team already trusts, so anyone reviewing the evidence sees familiar shapes and stops asking questions.
takeaways: An email attachment is still the most common way this kind of intruder gets in.
Familiar looking traffic is not proof of safe traffic, so check the behaviour too.
Unusual services and startup entries on a computer are worth investigating.

objectives: Explain what infrastructure imitation means and why it complicates threat detection.
Describe the spear phishing delivery routes that public reporting associates with Mofang.
Explain why compressing and encrypting a payload defeats simple attachment scanning.
Identify endpoint evidence such as new services, registry run keys and application shim entries.
Assess how regional targeting affects the detection rules an organisation should prioritise.
